issues.title: Define the serialNumberHash + CertHash as truncated hashes
issues.author: highlunder
issues.body:
From the meeting: we don't want to spend 32 byte on serialNumberHash/CertHash, but rather use truncated versions.

[What format/standard should we refer to? Something similar to kid = first 8 bytes of SHA-256(pubkey)?]

comments.author: highlunder
comments.body: Related question: In my quick experiments, I have trouble reproducing the OCSP example identity SHA-256 hashes. Can you share the exact bytes for which the hashes are produced?

comments.author: lijun-nio
comments.body: I think truncated hash is OK. But I am not sure truncating hash to 64 bits is still secure enough.

comments.author: lijun-nio
comments.body: I registered now two truncated hash algorithms, SHA256/160 and SM3/160 which take the first 20 bytes of the original output. Using shorter (e.g. 8 bytes) may have security problem (I am not sure). Since the collision rate to have two serial numbers (1-20 bytes) is too high (e.g. 2^-32 for 8 bytes hash value).

comments.author: lijun-nio
comments.body:
> Related question: In my quick experiments, I have trouble reproducing the OCSP example identity SHA-256 hashes. Can you share the exact bytes for which the hashes are produced?

The original serial numbers can be extracted from the X.509 OCSP Requests and Responses. E.g. for the examples in section `Simple OCSP Request Example`. The serial number can be extracted via the command `openssl asn1parse -i -in file.pem` with output
```
~% openssl asn1parse -i -in x509ocspreq.pem 
    0:d=0  hl=3 l= 149 cons: SEQUENCE          
    3:d=1  hl=3 l= 146 cons:  SEQUENCE          
    6:d=2  hl=2 l= 109 cons:   SEQUENCE          
    8:d=3  hl=2 l= 107 cons:    SEQUENCE          
   10:d=4  hl=2 l= 105 cons:     SEQUENCE          
   12:d=5  hl=2 l=  13 cons:      SEQUENCE          
   14:d=6  hl=2 l=   9 prim:       OBJECT            :sha256
   25:d=6  hl=2 l=   0 prim:       NULL              
   27:d=5  hl=2 l=  32 prim:      OCTET STRING      [HEX DUMP]:32538E7485BD37AE454F1F0D2B9755D758B91F6E8E3A7AF397A0F400605C6FF8
   61:d=5  hl=2 l=  32 prim:      OCTET STRING      [HEX DUMP]:CC11C8740A0509EC4DA14CE5886E72364C0F63B60ED6347F13C16EE725B766A2
   95:d=5  hl=2 l=  20 prim:      INTEGER           :1234123412341234123412341234123412341234
  117:d=2  hl=2 l=  33 cons:   cont [ 2 ]        
  119:d=3  hl=2 l=  31 cons:    SEQUENCE          
  121:d=4  hl=2 l=  29 cons:     SEQUENCE          
  123:d=5  hl=2 l=   9 prim:      OBJECT            :OCSP Nonce
  134:d=5  hl=2 l=  16 prim:      OCTET STRING      [HEX DUMP]:11111111111111111111111111111111
```

 And then you may verify the SHA-256 hash value via `echo -n "1234123412341234123412341234123412341234" | xxd -r -p | sha256sum`.

comments.author: lijun-nio
comments.body:
For a simple (usually unsigned) OCSP request : we have 2 hash values (issuerCertHash, serialNumberHash), and
for a simple (always signed) OCSP response: we have 3 hash values (issuerCertHash, serialNumberHash, responderCertHash).

For the serialNumberHash, the hash (algorithm) must be cryptographically secure. But for the issuerCertHash and responderCertHash, we may use shorter hash value (e.g. 8 bytes), it is used to identify the corresponding certificate among small certificate pool.

comments.author: marco-tiloca-sics
comments.body:
Analogous content about CRL and the CRL Distribution Points is at https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc5280/#section-4.2.1.13

If only HTTP is used, the same things as in RFC 6960 and RFC 5280 can be said for messages that transfer C509-related information (e.g., about the request method that can be used).

At the same time, when querying an OCSP server, it should be the case that a caching-oriented, idempotent, and safe request is actually desired (in contrast with a POST request), while also not resorting to encoding the request content in the query component of the target URI of a GET request. So, if CoAP is used at all, the following can be considered:

* If both the server and the client use CoAP, requests can then use the FETCH request method (RFC 8132), with all its advantages compared to the stretched use of POST (or of GET with query parameters).

* If not both the server and client use CoAP (likely, the server is the one that uses HTTP) and a cross-proxy is deployed in between, we need the requests to be GET or POST (with the resulting downsides discussed in RFC 8132), since there is no defined translation between FETCH and a corresponding HTTP method (one day, the recent QUERY could be considered, see RFC 10008).

Regarding security and the current era, it's probably about strongly discouraging unsecure communication, whatever the transfer protocol used.

A few things to consider if cacheability of responses is desired:

* For OCSP requests, they should practically need to converge on nonce=null in order to set the ground for producing a cache hit.

* If OSCORE-based security is used, cacheability of responses is possible by using the variant of Group OSCORE defined in https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-core-cacheable-oscore/

comments.author: highlunder
comments.body:
Thank you Lijun & Rikard! A few inputs from the constrained-IoT side, now that I'm (partially) back from summer vacation :)

About the motivation / "industry need" / "comparison with alternatives":
 
I think we can state the gap (more) concretely, to make it clear that for constrained devices over 6LoWPAN/LPWAN, the practical alternative today is often no revocation at all. DER X.509 CRL and HTTP-based OCSP are too large and too many round-trips for the link budget. Framing the contribution as ~"enables [standard based] revocation where it was previously impractical" is a stronger claim, but justified, in addition to "smaller and easier to process" alone.

About CRLite, and possibly as a broader conclusion for the alternative section: The section already notes CRLite as a compressed, browser-oriented filter, which functions as client-side, non-interoperable local structures. And this is why a standard, certificate-type-agnostic wire format for full per-certificate status structures is a missing piece, which doesn't compete with CRLite but rather complements it. 

Multi-vendor point, agreeing with your comment Lijun: Even single-operator constrained deployments are in need of mixing silicon and/or stacks, so reusing standard, open-source-friendly modules (one C509 parser, COSE signatures, OSCORE) should be the way forward also there. Maybe also worth a sentence in the motivation.

On OAuth/token status lists: agree they target a different problem (issuer-assigned index over a bounded population) and aren't a like-for-like alternative, so I wouldn't expand the section for them. 

Related / FYI: I'm looking into a first implementations, let's soon discuss what we want a reference implementation to demonstrate!

issues.title: Hash algorithm
issues.author: lijun-nio
issues.body:
In the current draft, we register our own hash algorithms.

Another direction is to use the algorithm codes defined in COSE algorithms (which is a collection of all algorithm types, including hash, signature, encrytion, KDF, ...).

Discussion and decision is needed.

 @marco-tiloca-sics @rikard-sics @highlunder  @comsats

comments.author: rikard-sics
comments.body: I feel like reusage is the best choice whenever possible. Will have a look and follow up with a longer comment

comments.author: marco-tiloca-sics
comments.body:
TL;DR: My impression is that the current structure of the registry "C509 Hash Algorithms" is as intended and aligned with other registries in the new C509 ecosystem.


Looking at the new registry "C509 Hash Algorithms" defined in the draft:

* In spite of its name, its entries don't indicate only hash algorithms, but rather a bundle of information about hash algorithms.

  At the same time, it's really aligned with the spirit of other C509 registries, e.g., "C509 Signature Algorithms" [1] that has the same fields with reference to signature algorithms.

* Like for the registry at [1], I thought that the intent was to be able to use also algorithms that are not registered in the "COSE Algorithms" registry [2].

  E.g., for "C509 Hash Algorithms", see the entry with 'Value' = 3 for "SHA-224"; for "C509 Signature Algorithms" [1], see the entry with 'Value' = 8 for "SM2 with SM3".

  If the idea is instead to limit the C509 Hash Algorithms specifically to hash algorithms that are also registered in the "COSE Algorithms" registry [2] (although I haven't had that impression so far), then their 'Value' in the "C509 Hash Algorithms" could indeed use the same value that the corresponding algorithm has in the 'Value' column of the "COSE Algorithms" registry [2] (e.g., -16 for "SHA-256"). However, thinking of fields like 'hashAlgorithm' defined in the draft, this also results in having less control when it comes to prioritizing values according to the most efficient, desired encoding in CBOR.


[1] https://www.iana.org/assignments/cbor-encoded-x509-c509#c509-signature-algorithms

[2] https://www.iana.org/assignments/cose#algorithms

comments.author: lijun-nio
comments.body: Any other thoughts or preferences？If we choose the cose algorithm table, I need also to update the test vectors before 2. Nov.

comments.author: lijun-nio
comments.body:
Here a overview of algorithms registered in this draft:

| This ID | COSE |
| --- | --- |
SHA-224 | ❌
SHA-256 | ✅
SHA-384 | ✅
SHA-512 | ✅
SHA3-224 | ❌
SHA3-256 | ❌
SHA3-384 | ❌
SHA3-512 | ❌
SM2 | ❌
SHAKE128 | ✅ 
SHAKE256 | ✅ 

SHA-224 and SHA3-224 are not important, we can remove the support of them. What we need are SM2 (for Chinese market) and the SHA3-family.

comments.author: xipki
comments.body: I prefer to use the COSE hash algorithm. One important reason is the main C509 draft defines a COSE header 'c5t' of type COSE_CertHash which uses the COSE hash algorithms.

comments.author: lijun-nio
highlunder
comments.body:
Agree with moving to the COSE Algorithms registry (PR #21). It seems to keep consistency within C509: the C509 certificate draft already identifies hashes via COSE codes in c5t/COSE_CertHash. The C509‑specific registry is used for signatures and not for hashes.

On Marco's two points: (1) algorithms missing from COSE (SM3, SHA3*) would be handled by registering them in COSE, which the PR does; (2) the CBOR‑encoding‑efficiency concern is small/hopefully negligible for the constrained default — SHA‑256 stays a single byte, and I think only SHA‑384/512 would cost one extra byte.

From the implementation side this is a low‑effort change: I can re‑sync the Rust c509rev (and the Contiki‑NG C) implementation to the COSE codes and regenerate the size‑comparison tables, when there are updated test vectors to use.

comments.author: marco-tiloca-sics
comments.body: Thanks! I realize now that, due to the obviously intended use of c5t, registering wished but missing hash algorithms in the COSE registry was going to happen anyway. At that point, one more reason to reuse that same namespace. COSE all the way, then :-)

issues.title: Resolving the Name / #6.121 encoding ambiguity in C509 CRLs
issues.author: lijun-nio
issues.body:
**In draft-ietf-cose-cbor-encoded-cert:**

```
Name = [ * RDNAttribute ] / SpecialText

SpecialText = text / bytes / tag
```

**In this draft**, the CRL structure has the following definitions:

```
authoritySubject       : Name / #6.121(bytes),

issuer                 : Name / #6.121(bytes) / null,
```

This creates an ambiguity. `#6.121` (the tag for alternative 0) is meant to mark a DER-encoded X.509 name, but because `SpecialText` allows `tag`, the same encoding can also be parsed as a `Name`. I see two ways to solve this:

**Option 1: Update draft-ietf-cose-cbor-encoded-cert.** Specify that a name consisting of a single commonName, which is currently encoded using the tag alternative, is instead encoded as `[ * RDNAttribute ]`.

- Pros:
  - Names in certificates and CRLs use the same encoding, so they can be matched byte for byte.
- Cons:
  - Requires a change to the C509 base specification.

**Option 2: Define a new CDDL type in this draft**, e.g. `RDNAttributes`:

```
RDNAttributes = [ * RDNAttribute ]

authoritySubject       : RDNAttributes / #6.121(bytes),

issuer                 : RDNAttributes / #6.121(bytes) / null,
```

- Pros:
  - No change to the C509 base specification is needed.
- Cons:
  - If a certificate's Name consists of a single commonName attribute, it must be re-encoded before it can be compared with the CRL's name.

Which option would the you prefer?
@marco-tiloca-sics @highlunder @comsats 

@rikard-sics : Maybe we could bring this up during the COSE WG presentation?

comments.author: rikard-sics
comments.body: Yes we could raise this during the IETF 127 presentation and see if the WG has any preferred solution

comments.author: marco-tiloca-sics
comments.body:
At this stage of the process, I easily prefer Option 2: it avoids changing draft-ietf-cose-cbor-encoded-cert and it is "cleaner" as it defines what the data model needs here (acknowledging that a non-ambiguous reuse of `Name` is not possible). Sure, the mentioned re-enconding is not nice.

However, the change proposed as Option 1 is about forcing the use of `[ * RDNAttribute ]` for a name that consists of a single commonName.

Can't the same reasoning be incrementally applied to Option 2 and evolve it into the following Option 3?

```
RDNAttributes = [ * RDNAttribute ]

authoritySubject       : RDNAttributes,

issuer                 : RDNAttributes / null,
```

In other words, if it is in principle acceptable that C509 certificates could use the tag alternative instead of using `[ * RDNAttribute ]` also for a name consisting of a single commonName, can't the same be acceptable for the CRL structure here? Is this perhaps a backward compatibility issue for CRL responders?

comments.author: lijun-nio
comments.body: Option 3 does not provide the option to support X.509 Name.

comments.author: marco-tiloca-sics
comments.body:
Thanks, got it (and, of course, X.509 Name is not in the scope of draft-ietf-cose-cbor-encoded-cert).

Then `#6.121(bytes)` needs to stay around to ensure that the compact CRL structure works also when X.509 certificates are involved.

pulls.title: Initial reference implementation for CBOR Encoded Certificate Revocation Management
pulls.author: highlunder
pulls.body:
## Summary

This PR contributes **`c509rev`**, an open-source Rust reference implementation of the **C509 CRL** and **C509 OCSP** structures defined in this document: encode, decode, sign, verify, and the PEM textual representation. Correctness is checked by byte-exact known-answer tests against the draft's worked examples. The crate is self-contained and lives as the `c509rev/` subdirectory. This setup is mirroring the format `c509_demo_impl/` used for `cose-wg/CBOR-certificates`.

## Coverage

- **C509 CRL** — `CRLInfo` plus per-issuer revoked/removed entries with fixed-width, binary-searchable entry packing; delta and indirect CRLs; forward-delta `nextUpdate`.
- **C509 OCSP request** — Simple, Unsigned, and Signed.
- **C509 OCSP response** — Error, Basic, and Simple.
- **Signing / verification** — Ed25519 and ECDSA with NIST P-256, over the CBOR TBS.
- **PEM textual representation** — RFC 7468 `-----BEGIN C509 CRL / OCSP REQUEST / OCSP RESPONSE-----` for all three object types (RFC 4648 base64, no extra dependency).
- **Experimental** — a C509 Status List primitive, as a compact complement to the CRL.

## Validation

- Every draft worked example **decodes and re-encodes byte-for-byte**, including the original signature bytes (deterministic-CBOR round-trip).
- For signed objects, the encode KAT is a **TBS byte-match**, because the draft ships no example signing keys. In addition, the published `crlocsp-ca` Ed25519 key reproduces the exact `signatureValue` of the no-revoked CRL example — a full cross-implementation check — and is verified against the published CA public key.
- Ed25519 and ECDSA-P256 sign↔verify round-trips, with tamper and TBS-change rejected.

## Dependencies, layout, and licensing

- **Self-contained.** Depends only on `serde_cbor`, `sha2`, `hex`, `ed25519-dalek`, and `p256`, with **no dependency on the C509 certificate crate**. The few primitives it reuses — a deterministic CBOR encoder, the two v1-profile signature-algorithm ids, and Ed25519/ECDSA-P256 TBS signing — are carried locally (`src/lcbor.rs`, vendored verbatim under BSD-3-Clause with attribution; `src/registry.rs`; `src/sign.rs`), so it builds in a fresh clone with no sibling checkout.
- **Layout.** The crate lives as the `c509rev/` subdirectory, mirroring `c509_demo_impl/` in `cose-wg/CBOR-certificates`.
- **Licensing.** BSD-3-Clause.

## Robustness and security

- The decoder is hardened against malformed input: `revokedCertsControl.serialNumberLength` (`1..=20`) and `dateLength` (`0..=8`) are range-checked per the draft CDDL **before** they size entry strides and per-entry sub-slices (an oversized value could otherwise panic — a DoS), and `baseDate + offset` uses checked arithmetic.
- A **"Security considerations & known limitations"** section in the README records what was reviewed sound (no `unsafe`; CBOR parsing returns errors rather than panicking; sound signature verification) and the remaining items: residual CDDL value-range checks are a tracked conformance TODO; `serde_cbor` is unmaintained (RUSTSEC-2021-0127); and the 8-byte identity-hash truncation is a draft-level size/security trade-off.

## Testing

- `cargo test` — **45 passed, 0 failed, 0 warnings** (known-answer tests, decoder-hardening regression tests, and PEM tests including the RFC 4648 base64 vectors and PEM round-trips over the draft's worked CRL/OCSP examples).
- `cargo build --all-targets` — clean, 0 warnings.
- `cargo audit` — 0 vulnerabilities; the only advisory is the documented `serde_cbor` unmaintained notice.
- CLI (`bin/c509rev`) — `decode` / `verify` / `pem`, with hex- or PEM-encoded input auto-detected.

## Status

Reference and test tooling — not for production use. The implementation tracks the current draft revision and is intended to stay in sync as the specification evolves.

pulls.title: c509rev: enforce the 16..32-byte OCSP nonce and refresh the README
pulls.author: highlunder
pulls.body:
Follows a6d1b1a and brings the README up to date with the draft. 

`cargo test`: 46 passed, 0 ignored, 0 warnings.

- **Nonce length.** a6d1b1a constrains the OCSP `nonce` to `bytes .size (16..32)`, and the Security Considerations require implementations to reject input that does not conform to the CDDL. The decoder now rejects a non-null nonce shorter than 16 or longer than 32 bytes as `Malformed`, in all OCSP request and response types. New test: `nonce_length_is_enforced`. The draft examples use 16-byte nonces, so the known-answer tests are unchanged.
- **README.** Rewritten to state what the crate supports, what it does not, and how it validates input, with the known gaps. This corrects some stale statements.

No other behaviour changes. `cargo test`: 41 passed (the 4 removed tests were the status list's own), 0 warnings.

pulls.title: draft: one modification and one addition to Security Considerations
pulls.author: highlunder
pulls.body:
Two potential small additions to the Security Considerations section, each independent of the other, so either can be dropped.

1. **Signature Verification: deterministic encoding.** Verifying the signature over the bytes as received becomes a MUST (was SHOULD), and a message that is not deterministically encoded (the Terminology section already defines "CBOR" as deterministically encoded CBOR) MUST be rejected. Otherwise implementations can interpret the same signed bytes differently, and values computed over the encoding, such as cache keys, are not stable.

2. **New subsection Certificate Status.** `not-issued` and `unknown` do not assert that a certificate is valid, and a relying party MUST NOT treat them as `good`. A responder that knows that a serial number was not issued SHOULD return `not-issued` rather than `good`. This is a SHOULD because RFC 6960, Section 2.2, allows `good` for a serial number that was never issued.

comments.author: rikard-sics
comments.body:
Considering that there is still discussion and open points regarding this PR, I would propose not merging it before submission of the next version.

Thoughts?

comments.author: highlunder
comments.body:
> Considering that there is still discussion and open points regarding this PR, I would propose not merging it before submission of the next version.
> 
> Thoughts?

As long as the rest of you are either ok with the current SHOULD, or don't foresee major problems changing it later if we so decide, I don't mind either way!

comments.author: marco-tiloca-sics
comments.body:
At a high level:

* Keeping the "SHOULD" instances is fine for now, and it might even be good in the long run (as long as more text around it is added). See more comments inline to the proposed changes.

* At the moment, no need to rush with merging this PR. We can think more about it.

comments.author: rikard-sics
comments.body: Okay, I will take a decision to submit now without this PR. We can of course include it (modified or not) in the next version

Suggestion to avoid avoid ambiguities:

OLD
The signature MUST be verified over the bytes as received rather than over a re-encoding.

NEW
The input to the signature verification process MUST be the bytes as received rather than the result of a re-encoding.

I'd like to keep the (left) original text.
1) A message that is not deterministically encoded ... MUST be rejected --> This requires additional checks, and the receiver is usually lean while parsing messages.
2) We do not limit how an application verifies the signature, give just suggestion here.

> An OCSP responder that knows that a serial number was not issued by a recognized issuer SHOULD return `not-issued` rather than `good`.

In the reality many OCSP responders use CRL as the status source, and will consider an issuer number not in the CRL as "good". With the text above we may have problem in this case.

If the first "MUST" about the signature verification becomes a "SHOULD" again, we should have additional text that gives acceptable reasons to deviate (i.e., to do re-encoding of what was received) and under which circumstances.

If the second "MUST" about rejecting what does not use deterministic encoding becomes a "SHOULD", then:

* We could keep the already present text "otherwise, implementations ..." to clarify the consequences from deviating.

* We should add text that gives acceptable reasons to deviate and under which circumstances. This would also be consistent with the expectation set in Section 3 that, unless otherwise stated, "CBOR" refers to deterministically encoded CBOR.
That suggests that a "SHOULD" is appropriate then, as there are actually existing cases of deviations where "good" is returned. Then it would be good to state those reasons.
